body_text: It’s a boom time for Advent calendars, with wholesale sales of the countdown-to-Christmas products up 63% year over year. The holiday tradition, where kids can get perhaps a chocolate or a small toy each day in the season of Advent ahead of the big day, has wound up at the confluence of a couple of major toy-industry trends . What is an Advent calendar if not 24 blind boxes you get to crack open? Is the thrill not the same as that of opening up a trading card pack or a video game lootbox? And with adults now buying most of the toys for themselves, anyway, what could play better to a “kidult” audience than an ostensibly religious way to give yourself toys for a whole month? Coreweave had a wild week, with anxieties about its debt spurred by a rather candid comment by one of its founders — and stoked by Elon Musk — spiraling into a broader moment of anxiety around just how much money the AI revolution is requiring investors to put up. A full-court press from CoreWeave’s boosters appeared to reset expectations , but where does this all leave us as we assess the state of the AI trade? CoreWeave shares sold off as much as 15% on Wednesday after a remark from a cofounder about the company’s attempts to get an investment-grade rating that would allow it to borrow from insurers rattled markets, with the executive describing the capital as “unlimited, like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche.” That put a bit of a spotlight on the company’s debt situation, as the 2031 CoreWeave bonds yield 15%, which is very very high for a company in its position. Well, amid the renewed scrutiny the cost of protecting that debt against default for five years rose to 1,194 basis points , 74.5 basis points in a day, swaps pricing in a 60% chance of default within five years. Wow , one might think, even Elon Musk is worried about the AI bubble? No. No he is not. Don’t be ridiculous. Elon Musk simply owns a competitor: SpaceX is rapidly attempting to build out large AI data centers that can both reduce its reliance on — and ultimately compete with — neoclouds like CoreWeave. In fact, as Grok and the other products of SpaceX’s AI lab continue to lag rival products out of Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet , Meta and so on, the core shareholder value of SpaceX’s AI business will be the neocloud element that can eventually sell compute to those winning teams. Remember, SpaceX cut a $1 billion a month deal to sell compute in September, which of course leads to the question of “why does SpaceX have excess compute?” Elon’s “yikes” is, if anything, more kicking a rival when they’re down rather than any concession that the technology he has tied his fortune to has issues. So, where does that leave us? Well, CoreWeave stock finished up 5% Thursday, still down 17% over the five-day, with its CEO waving the week away saying “there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” The unique cultures of Silicon Valley and Wall Street have been in general alignment that the AI boom is going to make a lot of people a lot of money. But before we get cocky, it’s worth remembering two axioms held as truth in either camp that apply very well : From the West coast: the future is already here — it's just not very evenly distributed. From the East coast: markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent. The AI boom’s benefits to shareholders will not necessarily be evenly distributed. If, for instance, there are one or two models that get a lot of pickup or achieve milestones faster than rivals can achieve, even companies that get lots of money in investment will not be worth a whole lot. If the world runs all its AI out of data centers, the neoclouds win; if, on the other hand, we don’t need all these buildings and you can eventually run a solid model on a phone, then the neoclouds will bite it. Heck, maybe free Chinese open source models can do 97% of the work of AI, and the American labs become boutique R&D firms arguing with academics over whether they actually solved theoretical math problems. In short: There are lots of worlds in which both LLMs are popular, useful technologies integrated into the American economy, and also some of the companies getting high valuations don’t exist anymore. Sure, which companies win and which companies lose that future could be decided by breakthroughs in AI model development or a phalanx of Nvidia chips powered by fusion power or a data center deployed to space, or any of these big and exciting reasons that a company might win that investors like to imagine. But for lots of them, their victory or their death will be decided by the rather boring parts of the balance sheet describing how much money they owe creditors in 2032. Whether this week was actually the axis upon which the AI trade turns is a bit premature. But it is the shape of things to come, a taste of what the future will at some point bring, at least when everyone flips their cards on the table and the winnings get divided. Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it. Just ask Character.ai . Unsurprisingly, this year’s movies are playing a big part in the trending outfits of 2026, with Agamemnon from “The Odyssey” in fourth; Nikki from “Obsession” in third; and Buddy the Unicorn, the titular character from the viral horror phenomenon “Buddy,” taking first. Never mind that it’s yet another screen to add to your roster! Never mind that “iPad” might just have been the perfect name for an Apple home hub had it not been taken in 2010! Just be happy that you now have a new option in the crowded market of big tech smart-home products to choose from, after Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday. Dubbed a “new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home,” the 7-inch, $299 device will officially drop on Friday, November 13, per the company’s announcement . From the chaotic three-minute trailer, users will be able to play music, control smart devices, FaceTime hands-free, and access Siri AI — basically everything you can do from any number of the smaller Apple devices you already own, cementing the pithy “ It’s an iPhone for your home .” verdict from The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. Alongside another device to take to battle against Google and Amazon equivalents, Apple also announced new HomePod smart speakers, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and a suite of smart-home accessories made in collaboration with LG. Increasing its offering of devices to dot around the house makes sense when taking a look at its Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories segment more broadly. The division that covers AirPods, Watches, TVs, Beats, and accessories like chargers and cases has seen revenues sink a little in recent years, with sales down some $3.2 billion in the first quarter of the year compared to their 2022 peak. It’s important to note that even with the declines more broadly, Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories unit still hauled $7.9 billion for the company in Q3 — putting it slightly behind Macs ($10.4 billion), slightly ahead of iPads ($6.2 billion), and contributing 7.6% of the company’s overall revenues for the quarter. With reportedly soft sales for the company’s latest iPhone and the big bet it’s placed on its soon-to-be-released foldable Duo not yet a surefire success, could the company’s new range of home products rise to the challenge and potentially help CEO John Ternus keep the Apple house in order? body_text: Somewhere between the invention of the internet and the rise of Wi-Fi, someone decided pigeons might be useful again. Back in 2001, Norwegian tech enthusiasts experimented with transmitting internet data via carrier pigeons. Of the nine packets sent, only four replies came back. Not exactly a technological breakthrough. But 25 years later, one of those packets is up for auction at Christie's , with bidding already reaching $4,000. Apparently, even a failed technology venture can appreciate in value. Stocks slid on Tuesday as US crude oil prices ticked higher while the global benchmark dropped. Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has spent the past five years looking for love in a hopeless place: the Nasdaq stock exchange. The company announced Tuesday that Ithaca Holdings , an investment firm founded by two Silicon Valley veterans that appears to be less than a year old, has agreed to buy it for $1.3 billion cash in a take-private deal. Shareholders will receive $6.05 per share, a whopping 138% premium to Friday's closing price, the last trading day before the Wall Street Journal reported Bumble and Ithaca were in advanced talks. The $1.3 billion price tag may sound like a lot until you remember the company had a peak valuation of about $14 billion around the time it went public in 2021. Bumble has seen its sales decline for the past few years and is expected to report a $15 million net loss for this fiscal year which would mark its fifth consecutive year in the red. It’s unclear exactly how Ithaca plans to turn it around. In a statement, Bumble CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd (who, notably, recused herself from the board vote on the takeover) said Ithaca is “a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future.” In case you forgot: Wolfe Herd founded Bumble as a women-focused dating app in 2014, she announced she was stepping down as CEO in 2023, then returned in 2025. Bumble — not unlike its peer apps owned by Match Group — has struggled to keep users engaged, particularly younger ones who are growing tired of endless swiping. Its paying user base shrank 16% year-over-year to 3.2 million in the second quarter , while revenue fell about 15%. The company has been trying to reinvent itself, loosening its signature women-make-the-first-move rule and experimenting with in-person events where users meet before matching. Its biggest planned change is doing away with the swipe altogether, although it hasn't revealed what will replace it. The new model is expected to begin rolling out in early 2027, following technical delays. The takeover also means a changing of the guard: Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta, a former Instacart executive, and John Hegeman, a former Meta executive, will become Bumble's co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd will remain involved with the company she founded. You need a big enough pool of people on your platform. Then you have to convince enough of those people to pay for premium features. And then, if those premium features actually work, you’re perpetually cannibalizing your own subscriber base. Not to mention the tides are turning away from swipe-based apps. Gen Z would rather touch grass and seek a meet-cute than brainrot on a dating app. While some startups are certainly trying , It’s unclear where Bumble or its peers squeeze shareholder value from in that world. 📊 Inflation: There’s a 50% chance that inflation comes in above 3.6% in September, according to prediction markets, with an 8% chance that it comes in even hotter at 3.7%. 🏛️ Senate: On a related note, we are now just three weeks out from the midterms, and markets are pricing in a blue wave.
